Something antediluvian is so incredibly old or outdated that it seems to belong to a completely different world — one that has long since vanished.

This word works on two levels — a literal one and a figurative one. Both are in active use, but the figurative meaning is by far the more common one today.

The literal meaning refers to the period before the Great Flood — the biblical event described in the story of Noah, where a massive flood is said to have covered the Earth and wiped out most life. So in its strict, literal sense, "antediluvian" describes creatures, civilizations, or events that existed before that flood. Paleontologists, theologians, or historians might use it this way when referring to ancient prehistoric creatures or early human societies.

The figurative meaning — which is how almost everyone uses it today — is an extended version of that idea. It describes anything that is so old, so outdated, or so behind the times that it feels like it comes from an entirely different age of the world. Not just old. Not just a little behind. We're talking about something that feels like it predates the modern world entirely.
The feeling and tone it carries

This is important: antediluvian is not a neutral word. It almost always carries a dismissive, mocking, or slightly contemptuous tone. When you describe something as antediluvian, you are not simply observing that it is old — you are implying that it is so hopelessly out of date that it has no real place in the present world. It often carries a touch of humor, like you're gently laughing at how absurdly ancient something is.

Think of it as saying: "This belongs in a museum — or better yet, a fossil record."

Very strong. It sits at the far end of the "outdated" scale. Consider this spectrum:

Old-fashioned → Outdated → Archaic → Antediluvian

Calling someone's phone an "old phone" is mild. Calling it antediluvian means you consider it so ancient and obsolete it's almost laughable. The word is deliberately exaggerated, which is part of why it's often used for effect — to emphasize just how far behind something is.

Here are examples that show the word in action across different contexts:

  • "His antediluvian views on women in the workplace shocked his younger colleagues."

(His views are so outdated they seem to belong to a completely different era.)

  • "The hospital was still running on antediluvian software that hadn't been updated in twenty years."

(The software is absurdly old and outdated for a modern setting.)

  • "She refused to give up her antediluvian flip phone, even as everyone around her switched to smartphones."

(Her phone is comically old by today's standards.)

  • "The professor's antediluvian teaching methods involved nothing but chalk, a board, and long dictation."

(His methods are so old-fashioned they feel prehistoric.)

  • "The fossil record shows that antediluvian creatures like mammoths roamed the Earth long before human civilization."

(Literal use — creatures from a very ancient, pre-modern era.)

It's easy to confuse it with similar words, so here's a clear distinction:

  • It is not the same as old. A ten-year-old car is old. It is not antediluvian.
  • It is not the same as classic or vintage, which carry warmth and admiration. Antediluvian carries criticism or mockery.
  • It is not the same as traditional, which is neutral or even positive. Antediluvian implies something is past its usefulness.
  • It is not always a factual statement about literal age — it is often hyperbole, used to dramatically emphasize how behind-the-times something feels.
Who uses this word and where?

Antediluvian is a somewhat formal and literary word. You'll find it in journalism, academic writing, novels, and educated conversation. It's not the kind of word you'd casually drop in a text message, but you absolutely might hear it in a speech, a newspaper opinion column, or a well-written novel. It's also occasionally used with deliberate humor — someone might jokingly call their own old laptop "antediluvian" to get a laugh.

If you ever see or hear the word antediluvian, your brain should immediately think: "This is describing something absurdly, laughably old or outdated — so far behind the times it might as well be prehistoric." The speaker or writer is almost certainly not being neutral about it; they want you to feel the weight of just how ancient or irrelevant this thing is.
